messages.mes:
The road did the work first. Ruts baked hard by dry days carried Alaric along the field-edge, past a drover prodding two gray geese ahead of a stick, past a cart heaped with cut firewood whose driver nodded the way country people nod at anyone on foot. The walls came up slowly, stone the color of old ash, patched in places with newer, paler masonry. Woodsmoke and something like onions drifted out from the gate on the wind.

Four guards stood under the gatehouse, spears leaned against their shoulders rather than level, watching traffic the way shepherds watch sheep. A man in armor with a sword on his hip drew a glance and nothing more; half the morning's traffic carried a knife, and some carried worse. The one nearest studied Alaric's face for a breath, found it young and unremarkable, and looked back at the road.

Inside, the city woke around him. A woman beat a rug from a first-floor window. Two boys chased a dog the wrong way down a gutter. The street smelled of horse, bread, hot iron from a smithy open to the air, all of it crossing under the sound of a hammer that rang and rang. Cart wheels ground over stone.

The Adventurers' Guild kept a sign where two streets crossed: a shield crossed with a sword, painted on a board that had weathered gray, an arrow carved beneath it pointing downhill. The way it marked followed the slope toward a long hall of dark timber built over a stone undercroft, its doors standing open to let out noise and the smell of tallow and wet wool.

Inside, morning light fell through high windows onto plank tables and the men and women at them. A long counter ran along the left wall, a gray-haired woman behind it entering figures into a ledger. On the right wall, sheets of paper covered a broad board, pinned in rows. Nobody looked up for more than a moment. A hunter's pack thumped down on a table. Dice rattled somewhere near the back.

messages.mes:
The counter's edge was worn pale where a hundred elbows had leaned. The gray-haired woman finished her ledger line before she looked up, then set the pen down in the gutter of the open book.

"Registration?" She said it without surprise; it was the question she heard most mornings. "Two silver. That's the one-time fee — covers your registration, your mark, and the slip. After that you're a Novice member, and you can take any contract posted at your rank or below."

She turned sideways and hooked a thin wooden board off the wall behind her, a slab of pale wood the size of a hand, sanded smooth. "You put your hand on the stone, it reads your measure — that's your Power Rank. That's separate from Guild standing, mind. The Guild doesn't grant strength; it only writes down what's already there. Rank F's where near everyone starts."

She set the board on the counter between them, then pulled a fresh ledger page toward her, pen waiting.

"Two silver, your name, and your touch on the stone. That's all there is to it." Her eyes went to the pouch at his belt and back to his face, patient, unhurried. Behind him a door thumped and two men came in talking about a fence line, boots leaving damp prints on the boards.

messages.mes:
The two silver coins crossed the counter with a small double click. The clerk swept them into a drawer, wrote *Alaric* into the ledger in a quick, practiced hand, and turned the board so the pale stone set into its center faced up.

"Hand flat. Hold it still."

The stone was cool under his palm for a heartbeat, then warm, a faint prickle running up through the fingers like the numbness of a limb waking. Somewhere inside the board something ticked, twice, and the warmth faded. The clerk lifted it, tilted it to the window light, and read the faint mark that had surfaced in the grain.

"F." She said it without ceremony, already reaching behind her. "Common as dirt, and no shame in it. Every name on that board above your head started the same place."

She set a small plate on the counter — dark iron, a hand's width, stamped with the Guild's shield and sword and a fresh-cut notch at its edge. "Your mark. Novice standing. Wear it or keep it in your pocket, but any Guild in the realm will know what it means. Lost plates cost to replace, so mind it."

She blotted the ledger line and closed the book partway. "Contracts are on the board, right where you came in. Novice takes what's marked for Novice or below. Read the slip before you take one — the proof it wants, the payout, all of it. You take it from me, you bring it back to me, and you get paid here. Anything else, ask."

Behind him the two fence-line men claimed a table, and one of the dice games swore at a bad throw.

The clerk took the slip, read the header, and gave a small nod. "Mossback. Level one." She stamped the seal into the soft wax at the bottom, pressed the ledger line flat with her thumb, and slid the slip back across the counter, the Guild's shield-and-sword now sunk dark red into the paper.

"That makes it yours. Nobody else takes it while you hold it — though the pencil note's true, two parties are working the upper tunnels already. You may meet them down there, or their leavings. Level one's goblin scouts and warriors, nothing worse has come up in weeks, but 'weeks' is not 'never,' so keep your eyes working."

She tore a strip from a memo pad and sketched quickly: a line for the quarry track, a knuckle for the mossy hill, a short stroke for the tunnel mouth. "Half a day east, off the old quarry track. You'll see the palisade stakes before you see the hill itself — goblin work, crooked, but it's there. Entry ledger's ours, so if someone's at the mouth, they'll have signed."

She pushed the sketch across. "When it's cleared, bring the slip back and we settle it here. Any Guild desk will do it too, if you end up nearer another city. Mind the wet rock under the moss — it's said the hill drains badly, and the moss hides what's under it."

She turned back to her ledger, pen already moving. Behind him, the dice game threw again and someone groaned.

messages.mes:
The east gate let him out past a knot of carters waiting on a wheel, and the old quarry track took over — two ruts hardened by years of iron-shod wheels, running through rough pasture with the hill country rising gray-green ahead.

The morning went by under a low, moving cloud. A drover passed him driving three shaggy cattle the other way and gave him a nod, nothing more. Farther on, the verge showed old mule dung and, once, a broad dark smear in the grass where something heavy had been dragged — a week old at least, rain-flattened, already growing through with weeds. He walked on. Toward midday the track climbed a shallow rise and the quarry opened on the left: terraced cuts in the hillside, tools stacked and covered, no one working it today.

The track bent around the quarry's edge and there the trees started — birch and alder, wet-leaved — and the ground went soft underfoot, draining badly just as the clerk had said. The stakes came before the hill, exactly as promised: crooked wooden points driven into the earth at odd angles, some leaning, some rotted to splinters, goblin work through and through. Beyond them the hill stood green from crown to foot, moss thick as a mattress on its flanks, and in that green a dark gap opened — the tunnel mouth, framed with fitted stones gone slick and black with damp.

An iron-strapped box was bolted to the rock beside the entrance. The ledger inside was damp-cornered but legible. The last lines read: *Hale, Wick — in yestermorn — out midday, level 1.* Below that, fresher ink, three names: *Brann, Otha, Whitlow — in this morning.* No time out written against them.

From the tunnel came the small industry of water — slow drips falling somewhere deep, striking stone. The dark past the first bend of the entrance gave back nothing else.

messages.mes:
The fitted stones of the mouth gave onto packed earth, and the gray light of midday followed him in for twenty paces before it thinned to nothing. The tunnel went on by feel and by sound: the slow drips striking stone somewhere ahead, the squelch of wet moss under his boots, the close smell of earth and something sourer beneath it, like a midden.

The warren bore its makers' marks plainly. Claw-scored walls where the digging had been hasty, a rib of root grown through the ceiling and hacked back, a flat stone set on end as a step over a puddle. Once, a chalk arrow on the rock, fresh enough to smudge — the morning party's marking, pointing deeper. He passed it and went on. The dark settled in around the drip-sound until it was the only thing, patient and even.

Then a different light, faint and orange, breathing around a bend in the tunnel.

He slowed. The bend opened into a wider cut where the tunnel forked, and in a hollow of the near wall burned a small fire — embers more than flame, goblin-tended, a rack of spitted mushrooms blackening above it. Three creatures sat around it. Knee-high, gray-green, big-eared, lean as whippets: goblin scouts, leather scraps strapped over their hides, short crude blades and a dart-stick lying to hand on the stones.

The nearest one saw him first. Its ears went up, its whole body went still, and it made a short barking sound — and the other two whirled, one snatching up its blade, one grabbing the dart-stick and half-rising, knocking the mushroom rack askew into the coals. Three pairs of eyes caught the ember-light and held on him, unblinking.

The fire hissed where the rack had fallen. None of them ran. None of them came on. The one with the dart-stick had it leveled now, arm shaking slightly with the effort of the aim, and the barker was edging sideways, putting the fire between itself and the dark shape standing in the tunnel with a sword on its hip.

Steel came out of the scabbard with a short scrape that carried down the tunnel, and the firelit hollow changed. The blade came up level, both hands on the grip, weight settled back onto his heels — a stance that said *come, then* without a word.

The goblins read it. The barker stopped its sideways edging and crouched, knees bending, fingers splayed against the stone. The one with the blade stopped flourishing it and held it low and close, point forward, the way a thing does when it has stabbed before. Only the dart-stick stayed level on him, the small arm behind it trembling, the creature's chest heaving in quick shallow breaths, its big ears flat back against its skull now.

Above the fire the fallen mushroom rack spat and smoked in the coals. The drips went on somewhere deeper, unhurried, as if the hill itself had no interest in the standoff at its fork.

The crouching one's weight rocked forward an inch, back an inch — a thing deciding. The dart-thrower licked its lips. Behind them the fork's far tunnel ran away black, and from somewhere down it came a second sound under the dripping, faint and rhythmic, that might have been digging or might have been footsteps, too far to tell.

None of them had moved past that rocking, coiled half-inch. The next instant belonged to whoever spent it first.

messages.mes:
Guard held, he came off his heels and stepped into the hollow, boots finding stone past the spilled mushroom rack — and the goblins broke like a kicked nest.

The crouching one, the barker, sprang sideways the moment his weight shifted, darting around the far side of the fire with its blade low, putting the coals between them. It moved fast, low to the ground, knees pumping, and fetched up behind the ember-light with its chest heaving.

The blade-carrier met him instead. It scrambled two steps forward onto the open stone, point leading, and made a quick stooping stab at his leading leg as he came in — a short reach, a short blade, the thrust falling short of him by a hand's width, the creature already hopping back on its haunches after it, out past his sword's line, ears flat, lips peeled back off its teeth.

Which left the dart-thrower. It had backed a step while the other two moved, and now its arm came back over its shoulder, dart-stick cocked, the ember-light jumping on its wide eyes. The small arm shook at the top of the throw, holding — a breath, two — and then the dart snapped forward.

The throw went wide. It cracked off the tunnel wall a foot left of his shoulder and spun away into the dark, and the thrower snatched at the second dart tucked in its leather strap, fumbling it, big fingers clumsy on the thin shaft.

The fire guttered between him and the barker. The blade-carrier circled a half-step to his right, testing the edge of his guard. Somewhere deeper down that far tunnel, the rhythmic sound came again — closer now, or he thought so — a dull knocking, stone on stone.

His blade was still up, still level, the Heavy Slash still coiled in his shoulders, unspent.

messages.mes:
It came fast and ugly, the way small vicious things fight.

The barker went first — a straight rush around the fire's edge, low and quick, and its blade raked across his forearm before his guard had fully settled. A hot thin line, the sting of it folding into the cold of the hollow. Then the big one, the one that had sat quietest at the fire, was off its stone and on him, heavier than the others by half a head, and its strike cracked against his ribs with real weight behind it, driving the breath short in his chest. The blade-carrier darted in under the same beat and nicked him across the thigh, a shallow tear through armor-gap.

He answered with the swing he had been holding. Heavy Slash came down off his shoulder in a full arc, steel hissing through the firelight, and caught the barker across the shoulder as it tried to twist away — a solid, meaty connection that knocked the creature spinning into the tunnel wall and left a dark wet stripe down its side. It rebounded off the stone, hissing through its teeth, blade still in its fist, blood streaking its leather scraps.

The big one hit him again while his arc finished — another blow across the same aching ribs, the second one folding him a half-step back. The wounded barker came off the wall snarling and slashed at his sword arm, opening the sleeve, the skin beneath. The blade-carrier darted in once more and bit another shallow cut into his leg.

His own breath came ragged now. Blood ran warm down his forearm and thigh inside the armor, and every rib on his right side reported with each pull of air. The fire spat. Three goblins ringed him at blade's length — the big one unhurt and steady, the wounded one leaving red smears on the stone it shifted on, the small one circling.

His sword came back up level. Whatever he did next was still his to choose.

messages.mes:
The retreat never happened. His boots stayed planted, and instead the longsword came up into full Guard, blade angled, shoulders squared behind it — a wall instead of a withdrawal.

The goblins came at it anyway.

The big one, Goblin Scout C, hit first and hardest, a heavy overhead chop that crashed against his raised steel and drove the shock down through both wrists into his elbows. The guard held; his bones did not much care. His arms rang with it, and the breath sawed thinner in his chest.

Then the wounded barker slipped in at the angle, quick as a ferret, and its blade skated along the edge of his guard and bit his forearm again — shallow, more insult than wound, but the blood was layering on blood there now, the sleeve wet through and sticking.

The blade-carrier came last, a darting probe at his hip that caught cloth and a line of skin, and skipped back before the point of his sword could answer it.

The hollow settled back into circling. Three of them, ringed at arm's length, their own breathing as quick as his. The fire had burned down to a red-bedded heap, and the light on the wet stone went dimmer, redder. His right side was a single dull ache from ribs to hip, his forearm slick inside the guard, and the sword point trembled — a small tremor, only a tremor — before he steadied it.

Down the far tunnel, the knocking came again. Closer. Neither goblin so much as glanced toward it; they had ears only for him.

The next move was his.

messages.mes:
He turned to run, and the ring closed before his second stride.

The big one, Goblin Scout C, hit him from behind — a full-weight blow across the back that drove him forward onto his knees, the sword spinning out of his blood-slick grip to skitter across wet stone. He got one hand under himself. The wounded barker took it across the shoulder, then raked him again as he crawled, and the blade-carrier came in last, low, unhurried now, and finished it.

The fire burned down to red ash. The knocking down the far tunnel stopped.

The three of them stood over him in the failing light, breathing hard, blood-spattered, and after a while they lost interest. The big one fetched his dropped longsword and turned it over twice, grunting, then tucked it under one arm and went to poke at the fire. The wounded one sat down on its stone and pressed a hand to its own shoulder, hissing. The small one crouched by the body and began, methodically, to strip the armor's straps.

The tunnel back toward daylight lay open and empty behind them, and nobody in the hollow was watching it.

Down that tunnel, on the wet stone of the level above, a Guild contract slip lay where its holder could not carry it any further. The Mossback Warrens went on being what they were: goblins in the dark, a shaman deeper down, and a guardian that still stood.
